headline: GPT-4o is retiring from OpenAI's API by January 14, 2027; multiple models affected
summary: OpenAI is deprecating GPT-4o, GPT-4o mini, GPT-4.1, and GPT-4.1 mini from its API. Developers must migrate to gpt-6-luna or other GPT-5.6 series models before the deadlines.
details: OpenAI has announced that GPT-4o, GPT-4o mini, GPT-4.1, and GPT-4.1 mini will be removed from its API on January 14, 2027. Any API calls to these models after this date will fail. This retirement affects API users, not ChatGPT users, as GPT-4o already left ChatGPT in February 2026.

The primary replacement for the GPT-4o family is gpt-6-luna, the smallest and cheapest model in the GPT-6 series. Custom fine-tunes of GPT-4o also follow the same January 14, 2027, shutdown schedule, with no grace period.

An earlier shutdown date of October 23, 2026, applies to the original May 2024 snapshot of GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-05-13), along with GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-4, GPT-3.5 Turbo, and other older models. These are being replaced by GPT-5.6-series models. Developers must check their exact model strings to avoid an earlier outage.

Additional deprecations include audio and real-time variants of the voice family shutting down on January 20, 2027, and transcription variants, including Whisper-1, on February 26, 2027. Developers should consult OpenAI's deprecations page for all specific dates.

OpenAI provided roughly three months' notice for these changes, which is shorter than its usual six-month standard for generally available models. This shorter timeline is typically reserved for safety or compliance concerns, though no specific reason was publicly stated.

The new gpt-6-luna model offers significant cost savings, with rates of $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, compared to GPT-4o's $2.50 and $10. However, token consumption differs between models, so actual costs should be measured on specific workloads.

GPT-4o is not being retired due to failure but as part of the industry's rapid model replacement cycle. Maintaining older models is costly, emphasizing that models are now disposable infrastructure, requiring developers to build for easy swaps.
caption:

headline_marked: [[The real cost of running LLMs on-premise]] is 40 hours of debugging, not power bills
headline: The real cost of running LLMs on-premise is 40 hours of debugging, not power bills
summary: On-premise LLMs can save on cloud API costs, but developers face significant hidden expenses in setup and maintenance. The true cost often comes down to dozens of hours spent debugging and optimizing infrastructure.
details: A logistics firm significantly reduced its cloud inference bill from $8,000 by moving LLMs on-premise. Initial power costs for a 24/7 GPU setup, serving over 100,000 tokens daily, were surprisingly modest, a fraction of equivalent cloud API spend.

However, the article highlights that the "free local inference" narrative often overlooks the substantial time investment required. While power bills are low, they do not represent the true total cost of ownership for self-hosted LLM projects.

The actual hidden cost includes approximately 40 hours of a developer's time over three months, spent on non-AI development tasks. This time was dedicated to resolving issues such as CUDA driver conflicts, Docker networking problems, and GPU memory allocation bugs.

On-premise LLMs are financially viable for specific usage profiles: high-volume repetitive inference, privacy-sensitive data, or workflows accepting "very good" rather than "state of the art" models. The economic breakeven for a $500-$600 GPU is roughly 3-4 months compared to $180-$240/month cloud costs.

For workloads under 100 calls per day, cloud APIs are generally more cost-effective when factoring in setup and maintenance time. The author gained valuable insights into inference engine memory allocation and Docker networking, knowledge acquired at a significant time expense.

A critical finding was that system RAM often becomes a bottleneck for 14B+ models with large context windows, even before GPU memory is maxed out. Upgrading system RAM proved more impactful for real-world throughput than many model optimizations.
